title: Agentic analytics with Power BI and Microsoft Fabric | OD817

segments.text: EMILY LISA: Hello, everyone.
We're excited today to talk about agentic analytics
with Power BI and Microsoft Fabric.
My name is Emily Lisa, and I'm a Principal Group Product Manager
at Microsoft.
SUJATA NARAYANA: And I'm Sujata Narayana.
I'm also a Principal Group Product Manager at Microsoft.
And we're really excited to get into some new innovation
and hopefully some things
that you guys will really enjoy seeing here.
EMILY LISA: Great.
So we will start off this session
with a quick introduction to the concept of agentic analytics.
Then we will go over in more detail end-to-end agentic
analytics with Power BI and Microsoft Fabric.
Then I'll hand it off to Sujata,
who will cover analytics with Fabric apps.
So to go ahead and get started,
what really is agentic development
for Power BI and Fabric creators?
What this really means is it's a way to use agentic experiences
with AI agents, skills, and MCP servers to help do all
of those different creator activities that you know
and love today, but with the power of AI using LLMs.
And so what we really are looking to support
with agentic development with Power BI is both greenfield
and brownfield scenarios.
So these are just simple examples,
but what we really mean by greenfield is those creating
from scratch experiences,
such as creating a net new semantic model, that you bring
in data, transform, do ETL on top of it, shape the model,
and then build a report afterwards.
Similarly, an example of a brownfield scenario is
when you're enhancing something that already exists.
So you might already have your Power BI semantic model
or your Power BI report, and there's some kind
of new requirement that comes in from your leadership chain
or a customer, and you want to adjust what you already have
to be in a shape that meets new incoming changes
and requirements.
So we can also help those scenarios
with agentic development as well.
So we're really looking to support both of these kind
of scenarios using AI to help experts do even more,
even faster than they can today.
And so let's take a look at what we mean
by end-to-end agentic analytics.
So, a few months ago, there was a GitHub repository
that was shared called Skills for Fabric.
And what this is is it's essentially a repository
that supports all sorts of different agent skills for all
of your different Microsoft Fabric scenarios for you
to be able to use agents to do all sorts
of different Fabric development tasks.
So this spans across things like lakehouses, notebooks, reports,
semantic models, really the whole Fabric ecosystem for you
to be more productive and move faster using AI.
And there's tons of flexibility with using this repository.
You could use it in all sorts
of different developer environments, such as things
like GitHub Copilot CLI or VS Code.
And this really helps you move even faster and allows you
to focus more on defining the context and really the
"why" behind what you're trying to create,
rather than spending hours and hours clicking
through every single step to implement the solution.
Really helps the LLM do some of that heavy lifting work
and allows you to focus on those high-level goals and outcomes.
And so we have this link here to try it out.
I'd highly recommend trying out the Fabric Skills repository
for all of your Fabric needs.
But what we really want to focus on here is how you can use this
for Power BI creation scenarios.
Starting with our modeling experiences, which we support
with the Power BI modeling MCP server.
Now, in the Fabric Skills repository,
there is a skill called Power BI model authoring.
And what this really does is help you craft your semantic
models in a way using natural language to really speed
up things that used to take a long time
through clicks or scripting.
Now you can do it easier
than ever using the modeling MCP server.
So the skill in the Fabric Skills repository calls the
modeling MCP server and has knowledge in the markdown files
to help you enhance your models to follow best practices.
And one additional enhancement on top
of that is we now make it easier than ever
to get started using the modeling MCP server
from the web modeling view.
All you have to do is click on the "Copilot" button
in web model view, and this will pop up a Copilot side chat
where you can use this to give your natural language prompts
to make changes to your semantic model, to make changes such as
to your DAX measures, relationships,
your column properties, all of those different rich semantics,
being able to modify them using natural language.
You can even get suggestions on how to make your model better
for your reports and optimize better for AI.
So you can both use all these really rich modeling experiences
in your developer environments,
and even coming soon in web modeling.
Now, the next skill that we support
in the Fabric Skills repository is the much-anticipated report
authoring skill.
We're really excited to ship this live
for the first time at Build.
And what this really does is help you both create net new
reports as well as edit your existing Power BI reports.
What this does is you use the PBIP file and desktop to be able
to create and edit your reports.
And it really helps you a lot of the heavy lifting
of all those operations that traditionally take a long time
with doing draggy, clicky, clicky,
draggy, droppy operations.
Now you can use natural language for all of them.
Some key things that you can do is update report themes based
on requirements, maybe even a screenshot,
as well as modify different visuals and report elements
to meet all the requirements that you have for your reports.
All right.
Well, enough talking about these skills.
Let's see what it looks like actually
in action with some demos.
So, in the first demo that I want to show, this is going
to be a greenfield scenario.
So in this case, I'm creating a net new semantic model
and report completely from scratch with the assistance
of AI using the Fabric Skills repository.
So here in my setup, I have
on the left-hand side an empty PBIP file open
in Power BI Desktop.
And on the right-hand side,
I have GitHub Copilot CLI connected
to this instance of Power BI Desktop.
Now, to create a net new semantic model within this file,
all I have to do is give a really simple prompt, such as,
"Create a new semantic model using data at ISQL database,"
and it'll just go ahead
and create this new semantic model for me.
I'm able to see all the changes validated on Power BI Desktop
on the left-hand side, while the LLM is also giving updates
of all the changes it's making on the right-hand side,
including a helpful summary.
Now I'm able to see I have a beautiful star schema,
but I want to take this one step further.
My organization defines our semantic modeling best practices
in a shared markdown file.
So I just give this file as context to the LLM and ask it
to update my semantic model to follow all
of those well-known best practices, which it goes ahead
and does for me, giving helpful summaries.
And I even see a description added
to my column matching the best practices.
Now, as a next step, I want to create a report off
of this semantic model.
What I do is I define each
of the report pages the requirements I have
for that page of what I want it to look
like within these two different markdown files.
And then I go ahead and give it as context to the LLM and say,
"Go and make this report for me."
And then what I'm able
to see afterwards is it creates this beautiful new report,
all based off of my written --
the requirements within my markdown files.
Now I want to take this one step further and style this report
to match theming and branding
that I desire for my organization.
So I give it a reference image of a sample report page
that I want the rest of my report to look like,
as well as my company's logo, for it to follow as theming
and styling best practices.
All it took was a really simple prompt and these two pieces
of information as context, and it was able to modify
that entire report for me to match all the styling
and theming guidance that I really wanted for this report.
All of these tasks, as many of you Power BI creators know,
often take many hours to do fine-tuning and clicking
and moving things around.
Now it's easier than ever, thanks to the help of AI
and the Fabric Skills repository,
making it so I could focus on defining the what of what I want
for my data solution, rather than going
through all the manual processes of making those things happen.
So that was a greenfield scenario, creating completely
from scratch using AI, a net new semantic model and report.
But as we talked about earlier,
it's not just greenfield scenarios we support.
We also support brownfield scenarios of being able
to edit existing things that you already have.
We know many of you already have existing semantic models
and reports that you either want to fine-tune
for new requirements or just want to modify based
on any new preferences you have.
Let's take a look at what a brownfield scenario looks
like for a report.
So in this case, I want to level up one of my existing reports
in one prompt using the same Fabric Skills repository.
Here, I have my report page,
which maybe could be a bit more visually appealing.
It's not following some of the reporting best practices.
I want to make it better and more executive-ready.
So all I do is I ask Copilot
to help improve my Adventure Works report.
I want to have a more modern feel,
have a clean editorial landing page
with intuitive page navigation,
and really look more polished and executive-ready.
In Plan mode in GitHub Copilot CLI, I'm given different options
of what this page can look like.
I review these and I go ahead and go with one of the options
that was suggested to me.
And then the LLM goes ahead and makes the changes
to my report based on that plan, and it looks beautiful
with consistent styling and theme.
I had that really nice landing page at the beginning.
This is in a much better state, where I'm ready to share it
with my executives and my larger team.
And it was so easy to get started, all in one prompt,
thanks to the assistance of the Fabric Skills repository
with the Power BI report authoring skill within there.
So that was really it for the end-to-end agentic analytics
part of the presentation.
Now I'm going to hand it off to Sujata
to cover the next section.
SUJATA NARAYANA: All right.
Thank you, Emily, so much
for showing us all the innovation that's happening
around agentic development in Power BI reports
and Power BI semantic models.
Now let's switch gears here a little bit, because I want
to talk about something that is brand new, in fact,
released just at this conference, which,
let's look at Fabric apps.
And specifically, I want to talk
about analytics use cases within Fabric apps.
So AI is really democratizing a lot that's happening
with web app development.
We're seeing all kinds of scenarios where MVPs
like Injae Park, Reid Havens are building end-to-end web apps
for enterprise analytics.
And because AI is making it so much easier to do this,
we're even seeing citizen developers being able
to achieve so much more here.
Now, where custom web apps add value beyond reports is
that developers that need more flexibility
or have higher custom requirements can really take
advantage of going the custom web app route.
Because with a custom web app, you're getting full custom UX.
So if you want things like responsive layouts,
unlimited UI controls, or even full-blown multi-step workflows,
you can get that with a custom web app.
And also, if you have scenarios
where you want fully customizable actions,
these web apps can be really helpful for that as well,
because you're getting a much more seamless integration
for building things like decision loops,
supporting custom code and custom integrations,
because at the end of the day,
custom web apps are all just code.
And now, here's the caveat.
Even though AI is democratizing a lot
of web app development today, the reality is that a lot
of these vibe-coded apps never reach production.
So majority of these apps, let's say if you built on Lovable,
Streamlit, or other surface areas, may not reach production
because they may miss things like enterprise-grade security,
governance, reliability, and more operational controls.
And so even though AI helps you get 80% of the way,
that additional 20% of making it ready for production,
if it's not there, it's just not enough to have
to your customers or your end users.
And so this is something that we want to tackle
with Microsoft Fabric.
And that's now introducing Fabric apps.
So you may have seen in some of the other sessions,
we made a huge announcement around Fabric apps,
which basically what that is, is a Fabric backend
for building enterprise-grade apps.
Now, let's talk about this a little bit more detail.
So what this is, is Rayfin is the project name,
which is allows for a CLI-based experience.
So not only is this developer-friendly,
but it's very AI-friendly too.
So here, you see an example from our NPM package,
which you can connect to your CLI experiences in order
to have your coding agent of choice be able
to build end-to-end apps that are all backed in Fabric.
Now, what does this relate to Power BI or semantic models?
Well, to start with, is Fabric apps can be built
on semantic models.
So that same foundation that you're getting
to build your reports from your analyst,
your developers can now build custom web apps on that as well.
And so what this unlocks is really good
for enterprise analytics.
So not only are you able
to build entirely blown custom web apps,
but these web apps are live -- using live data.
They are using optimized queries.
And, of course, we are using visuals that are very consistent
and meet enterprise-grade requirements while
being AI-first.
And by being secure connection to your Fabric data,
and also the enterprise scale and governance that you expect,
you can more safely deploy this
to your enterprise customers and end users.
So let's talk a bit about how to get started with this.
So Fabric apps includes a data app template.
So, to start with, is you can either choose the template
within the CLI experience.
So when you do your NPM create command,
you'll need to add a statement that says template data app.
Or if you're in Fabric, you can also initiate the creation of it
through Fabric as well.
So you can pick the template called Data App.
And let's talk a little bit
of what's happening behind the scenes.
So the data app template is really comprised
of three key things.
First is a data package that allows you
to securely connect to your Fabric data.
And next is a visual package,
which is using a Vega-Lite component and React components
so that you're getting visualizations
that are really optimized for AI, make it really great
for building a ton of different flexible visuals,
while also staying true
to certain enterprise-grade defaults.
And then, of course, we have a set of agent skills
that are helping teach the LLM how to properly query the data,
how to handle Fabric formats, write Vega-Lite visual specs,
and, of course, apply design best practices
so that these applications look really polished
and professional.
And all of these templates are built directly on Rayfin,
so directly on Fabric apps, so that you can leverage it
with your Rayfin experiences.
Now, let's take a look at a demo of what this looks like.
So let's see a scenario where I'm going to use a few prompts
and an MD file to generate a production-ready app.
So starting with my semantic model, you can see here,
it's using a lot of different tables,
a lot of different data here.
I want to take this data that is in the form of a semantic model.
I want to build an app from it.
So, to start with, is I'll have a spec
that actually AI helped me create around my requirements.
And even though AI helped me create it,
I can always go manually tweak this.
So here's an example where I want to add a hover card.
So let's say I want a image, an email.
I can go add those hover card tooltips there.
And the next part, I'm going to go scaffold that project.
So I use that NPM create command,
and I make sure I specify the template of data app.
So as you see here, the CLI experience is creating --
scaffolding the project for me,
and now I have the files all available on my local.
And so once I have this available,
I'm going to navigate to that file.
So if I go here, I navigate to my project file,
and then I'm going to go and publish this
to my Fabric workspace.
So, at this point, I've just provisioned the app.
I haven't yet created the exact app idea I have.
And this is where the fun part happens.
So, at this point, I'm going to give my coding agent
of choice a link to my spec file and a link to my semantic model.
So once it has these two critical details,
I ask it to go build the app and deploy it when it's ready.
So this takes roughly about 20 minutes or so
of your coding agent processing this request.
And when it's done, you get a full-blown production-ready
application that matches the requirements that you put
out in your spec. And so here, for example,
I have a three-page application here that includes things
like filtering, tooltips, like I mentioned, that hover card
that appears, even having more customization
like adding a full-blown dark mode.
And so it's really quite powerful of the type
of data application that you can create here.
Now, let's say you want to customize this even further.
And that's the beauty with working with AI,
is you really just need to update that MD spec.
So let's see an example of this.
So let's say I want to add a little bit more features
to this application.
Let's say I want a landing page,
I want persona-specific selection,
and I even want a calendar tab.
So I can go add all these requirements
to the spec and update it.
And then I just hand Copilot that updated spec.
So I just say, "Hey, update the app using the latest spec."
And as it's going to go process through that request again --
again, takes about 20 minutes or so,
and you have your updated application right here.
So you see the persona-specific selection.
So you have different set of pages for each persona.
So the executive page is a little bit more focused.
And then, of course, you have
that calendar view like I mentioned.
So this is really bringing in a lot more of actionable elements
to this application because I can now track the calendars
for the different collaborations I have coming up.
And I can even go and add those calendar events
to my Outlook calendar itself.
So you're really kind of combining the elements
of both the analytics with also the elements
of the action-orientated apps.
So it's really about bringing your data alive
and really customizing your app however you want,
and doing so in a prompt-based way.
So leveraging AI with what it's best for,
especially the coding agents, to really generate that code
from you, completely from scratch.
And so this is really showing the value
of what the data app template can offer as you are trying
out the new Rayfin and Fabric apps experience.
So now let's recap what you get with data apps in Fabric.
So, to start off with, is that connection
to semantic models is so critical.
Right out of the box, you're going
to get a secure authentication to your semantic models,
which I'm sure many of you have tons of semantic models
where you're eager to try this new experience with.
Next, you're going to get the AI-driven
analytics capabilities.
So out of the box, being able to have AI understand how
to write DAX queries,
making sure you're getting optimized queries
so that you're visualizing the right data, the right insights,
and, of course, formulating that really well in visuals.
And then speaking of our visuals, like I mentioned,
these visuals use the Vega-Lite visualization library,
which make it really easy to build AI-first visuals
and using enterprise-grade defaults.
And so we've added additional customizations on top of that
to make sure there's consistency in tooltips,
make sure there's accessibility,
and all the enterprise-grade requirements
that you would expect.
And more coming soon is that we want to add more sources.
So we know that there's a lot of other sources in Fabric
where you may not want to connect directly
to a semantic model, but you may want to connect directly
to other sources, let's say, a SQL DB directly,
or maybe a lakehouse or a warehouse directly.
So we do plan to add more sources coming soon.
We also want to have more out-of-the-box signal detection.
Of course, because web apps are just code, you can always prompt
that yourself, but we want to make it way easier for you
to get that signal detection right out of the box.
And same goes for custom actions as well.
So integration with things like user data functions,
integration with things like operational agents.
We want to enable a little bit more streamlined integration
with any sort of custom actions or custom agents that you want
to bring into the picture.
And last but not least, we want to make sure
that you also support embedded scenarios.
So in the first release -- right now, the data app is limited
to just being hosted within Fabric, and you see it
within the Fabric portal.
But we want to also make sure that in the future releases,
you can be able to embed this in your own application
or embed it in other areas.
So with that, we hope this gave you a good insight
into what we're doing in terms of innovation
for our analytics experiences,
both across Power BI and Microsoft Fabric.
And for those that are interested in learning more
about any of the things you've seen here check out our blog
at aka.ms/Azure-Data-Build26,
and also explore our documentation
and our community site to learn more
and engage with the community.
Thank you so much.
We hope you enjoyed this presentation and looking forward
to your feedback on all this new innovation.
